It does three things that are usually done separately. It describes a method for relating cultural material at the level of the story rather than the level of the organisation or the emblem. It applies that method to this archive's own recent output. And it draws proposals from the result that can be argued with, costed, or tested. Two honesties before anything else. First, the corpus is this site: 512 dated publications in the archive's own creation record, the index (513 once this page is counted; the window used here was computed before it existed), sorted by the timestamps the index itself stores. The window studied here is the twenty pages published on 25, 26 and 27 October 2026 that this document reads; the archive's index carries their dates, and the sources list them with those dates. Second, the word cult in section 7 is used in its technical sense — a high-control group , not "a religion someone dislikes". The distinction is defined there and is doing real work. Everything below that is a claim about a tradition cites an attestation: a text, a dated object, a documented practice. Where the evidence is a pattern rather than a datum, the text says "pattern". Where the claim is an interpretation, it says "reading". That vocabulary is not decoration; it is the difference between a comparative study and a horoscope. Read the twenty most recent pages by what they carry rather than by their subject, and the archive becomes a list of stories: the Uniform recurs, the Book recurs, the Road and the Gate recur, and the Dragon appears where the emblem is asked to do the work of a constitution. Nothing in the archive was organised that way — the pages were written one at a time, on different days, in two languages — and yet the same few machines keep appearing. Why memories and not symbols A symbol is a mark that stands for something: a flag, a logo, a pentagram, a crescent, a dragon on a coin. A memory , in the sense used here, is a narrative schema — a small story with slots in it: a threat, an agent, a remedy, a cost, and an obligation that falls on whoever hears it. The distinction matters because symbols are carried by groups and die with them, while schemas are carried by people and survive the groups that used them. Take the example that prompted this document. The dragon appears in China, in Mesopotamia, in India, in Greece, in Wales and in Mesoamerica, in forms that cannot all descend from one another. The question "which country invented the dragon" is therefore badly posed. The better question is: what schema is being filled , and who is holding it at a given moment? The schema is roughly: a great serpent controls water, weather or treasure; it must be negotiated with; the negotiation costs something; whoever can negotiate holds power . Chinese rain dragons are petitioned; the Vedic Vṛtra blocks the waters and is split open; Babylonian mušḫuššu guard the gate; Quetzalcoatl brings maize and is awaited. Four different politics, one story with the same slots. The four rules this atlas follows Relate the memory to the memory. Not "the Communist Party and the Catholic Church" but "the Chosen as a schema, held by a party in one century and by a church in another". Groups are hosts ; the schema is the thing that recurs. An attestation per claim. A route needs a text, an object or a dated practice. "This feels archetypal" is not evidence; it is the failure mode the method exists to prevent. Polygenesis is allowed. Similar schemas can be invented twice. The interesting cases are the ones where the slot structure is identical and the moral is inverted — that is usually transmission, and it is always information. The edge must be a transformation. Two memories are related when you can state the operation between them: feeds, inverts, absorbs, disguises, protects against. A relation you cannot state as a verb is a coincidence with good manners. The theoretical warrant for this is not Jung's collective unconscious, which is unfalsifiable, but three more modest bodies of work: Halbwachs and the Assmanns on collective and cultural memory (memory is stored socially, in institutions, calendars and texts); Sperber and Boyer on the epidemiology of representations (why some stories are catchy: they fit inferential defaults and are cheap to transmit); and Bruce Lincoln on myth as an instrument in the construction of society — that is, on the political work a story does when it is told at the right moment. None of these requires a universal psyche. All of them predict recurrence. The relations between memories are themselves the argument, and each is a transformation rather than a resemblance: the dragon feeds the flood, the flood authorises the chosen, the chosen requires the book, the book fixes the calendar, the calendar becomes a gate, the gate concentrates into a tower, and the tower provokes the next flood; the plague produces the scapegoat, the scapegoat escalates into the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is absorbed by the uniform, which is what lets a person carry out the expulsion without feeling it. Point the arrows the other way and you get conspiracy; state them as verbs and you get a testable claim. That is the whole difference between an atlas and a stamp collection. symbol → carried by a group, dies with it, means by convention memory → carried by people, survives the group, means by its slots host → whoever is holding the memory now (state, temple, party, firm, family) edge → a stated transformation between two memories (feeds, inverts, absorbs) 3. Water and sky — the Dragon, the Flood The Dragon — power that must be negotiated with Route. Dragon-like jades from the Hongshan culture in north-east China (roughly 3500–3000 BCE) are among the earliest surviving objects; the Babylonian mušḫuššu guards gateways; the Indian nāga rules rivers and rain; the Greek drakōn guards springs and hoards; the feathered serpent in Mesoamerica brings maize; the Welsh red dragon ends up on a flag. Whether these descend from one invention or were invented repeatedly is unresolved — and irrelevant to the method, which only needs the schema. What it asks. Tribute, a ritual, a maiden, a name. The dragon is the memory of a power that cannot be abolished, only bargained with — which is why it is the favourite emblem of every institution that wants to be bargained with rather than replaced. Hosts. The emperor (the dragon as the body of the state), the temple (the nāga as guardian of the law), the village (the rain procession), the firm (the logo). Where it turns harmful. When the bargain becomes hereditary: the dragon bloodline, the "dragon" that is simply the state and cannot be questioned. The emblem then does the work of a constitution without the inconvenience of one. In this archive the memory sits close to the emblem: GNR follows two dragons on a coat of arms across 225 years; Serpente reads a police force through the serpent it is named after; Macaco tells of a nineteenth-century monkey-dragon; Dragonfire and Sinais treat it as a voice rather than a beast; and Escuro with Dark give it its five phases and four symbols. The Flood — the water that erases and starts again Route. Atrahasis (c. 18th century BCE) and tablet XI of Gilgamesh ; Genesis 6–9; Manu and the fish in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; Deucalion in Greece; the fourth sun in Aztec cosmology; and Gun-Yu in China, where the flood is not a punishment but a problem of hydraulics, and the hero is the surveyor who dredges nine channels. What it asks. A verdict, or a works programme. The remarkable fact is that the moral is not stable: the same water produces a theology of judgement in Mesopotamia and a theology of engineering in China. Hosts. The priest (judgement), the engineer (canal), the party (the "cleansing"), the insurer (risk), the novelist (the fresh start). Where it turns harmful. When the flood becomes a licence: the purge, the slate wiped clean, the year zero. Every revolutionary who says "after the deluge" is borrowing the schema and skipping the ark. Revolucionário is the archive's own answer to the deluge — what to build before the water returns, and why purity is one of the three refusals; Ditador is the fantasy the flood invites; COMM-OS is a system promising a clean start; and Void is what a directive to the armed forces sounds like when the water is already rising. 4. Contagion and guilt — the Plague, the Scapegoat, the Sacrifice The Plague — the illness that makes a society visible Route. Athens in 430 BCE, described by Thucydides with a precision that still reads as reportage; the Justinianic plague of 541; the Black Death of 1347–51, which killed something between a third and a half of Europe; the influenza of 1918; and 2020, the first pandemic in which the counting was done in public dashboards. What it asks. Who is essential, who is contagious, who is to blame. A plague is the only event that forces a society to answer all three at once, in public, with money. Hosts. The board of health (the cordon), the priest (the procession and the penance), the mob (the pogrom of 1348–49), the platform (the dashboard), the insurer (the exclusion). Where it turns harmful. The plague finds a scapegoat before it finds a cause — and the scapegoat is usually the people who were already living at the edge of the camp. The Athenian pharmakos , expelled to purify the city. The medieval expulsion of the Jews after the plague. And René Girard's account of the surrogate victim, which is the most rigorous modern statement of the mechanism. What it asks. That one death restore the whole, and that the transfer be public . The rite is not the killing; the rite is the visibility. Hosts. The priesthood, the crowd, the party, the trending page, the commission of inquiry that needs a name. Where it turns harmful. It works. Culpa asks whose fault it is and finds monotheistic habits underneath the question; Vontade notices who is missing from the march; Masters names the most criminal group of all; and Jews follows the temptation to become equal by expelling someone. Moral injury is the moment a person discovers that the debt was somebody's decision, and that the "voluntary" was a form of words. The covenant and the election of Israel; the "city on a hill"; the caliphate as the community with the correct claim; the righteous king of the Buddhist mandala; the "civilising mission" of the nineteenth century; the vanguard party; and, in a minor key, the first users of any platform, who are always told they are the ones who understood it first. What it asks. Loyalty, purity, and the reading of history as a warrant. Election is always comparative: a people is chosen from something. Hosts. The temple, the nation, the party, the brand community, the family that "is not like the others". Where it turns harmful. The election of one group is the exclusion of another, and the exclusion does not need to be stated: it is the shadow the election casts. The pages on Bem and Good are the counter-file — people who refused the mandate and were right. Leaders is the inverted case — those who guided billions without a war; Absolute is the architecture of the leader who cannot be questioned; Teoricamente is the joke that names it; and the four files on warrant and refusal — Bem , Good , Mal and Evil — are what happens when the mandate is obeyed, and when it is declined. The Book — the canon that cannot be argued with Route. The Veda heard rather than read; the scroll and the codex; the canon of scripture fixed by councils; the constitution; the standard operating procedure; the terms of service. Every one of these is a text whose authority depends on who is allowed to interpret it. What it asks. That the reader be authorised. The whole politics is in the distance between the text and its reader: shorten it and you get literacy, lengthen it and you get a priesthood. Hosts. The scribe, the priest, the jurist, the moderator, the compliance officer. Where it turns harmful. When the text may only be quoted, never read; when the interpreter becomes the text. The dossier on Tendas is the sharpest local example: Scripture read as an inverted mirror, in which the Christians accused are the ones who do not follow Christ. The two experiments everyone cites are weaker than the citations imply: Zimbardo's prison study was partly coached, as the archived tapes showed, and Milgram's obedience experiments have been re-analysed and re-run with variations that narrow the original claims. The schema survives the corrections, because it was never really about the cloth. What it asks. That the person disappear into the role, and the role answer for the person. Hosts. The barracks, the department, the platform's anonymous handle, the call centre script. Where it turns harmful. Anonymity plus hierarchy plus a hostile script — the three together, not any one alone. The lunisolar month of the ancient Near East; the liturgical year; the computus, which is the original coordination problem of the Latin West; the French Republican calendar of 1793–1805; the Soviet five-day week of 1929 and the six-day week that followed; the ISO week; and the feed, which is a private calendar with a public interface. What it asks. That the group assemble on the same day, fast on the same day, and pay on the same day. A calendar is the cheapest machinery of coordination ever invented, and therefore the most political. Hosts. The priesthood (the feast), the state (the holiday), the employer (the deadline), the platform (the notification). Where it turns harmful. Whoever sets the holiday sets the economy; whoever sets the deadline sets the sleep. And a calendar is also a gate: the one who keeps the wrong day is outside. This operational paradigm is fundamentally flawed. Conducting war within an inhabited biosphere guarantees the destruction of vital ecosystems, clean water reserves, and arable soil. The resources expended to wage terrestrial warfare directly impair the planetary systems that allow human civilization to endure. The logic of national defense becomes inherently self-defeating when the methods of defense systematically ruin the land being contested. "To wage war within the ecosystem that generates your own oxygen and food supply is not strategic defense; it is systemic negligence." 02. The Asymmetry of Non-Combatant Harm The primary ethical breakdown of modern terrestrial warfare lies in the unavoidable target overlap between combatants and non-combatants. Despite advances in precision targeting, modern high-yield weaponry cannot isolate military actors from surrounding civilian infrastructure. Children, families, and innocent populations—who possess no formal agency in geopolitical mandates—bear the burden of military engagements. 90% Civilian Casualties in Modern Wars (UN Estimates) 100+ Years of Unexploded Ordnance Risk $2.4T Annual Global Defense Spending Soldiers operate under legal contracts and command hierarchies, fully aware of operational risks. mistica: Conversas Filosóficas Eu não conhecia o conceito, isto é, o nome que deram ao conceito, mas realmente é interessante. A minha curiosidade anda cada vez menor, há um excesso de informação e conteúdo, que hoje em dia eu já interiorizei, que o melhor na maioria dos casos é simplesmente registar a presença e sem sentir necessidade de entende-la. Estás a conseguir abstrair-te da necessidade de consumir conhecimento de forma compulsiva. Conhecer é bom mas não conhecer também o é. O bom de não conhecer, é que permite-te imaginar (mesmo que a errar) criando uma sensação mística. Essa sensação é interessante, mesmo fazendo parte da “ignorância”. No conteúdo tecnológico, por vezes tenho a impressão que as pessoas não aprendem propriamente nada, mas copia e repete, inttegrando os conceitos que já foram definidos. Também é interessante, principalmente se tencionas criar algo com o conhecimento que tens, mas caso não tenhas essas aspirações, é sem dúvida mais conteúdo que poderá criar “desassossegos”. Não concordo contigo na parte de criar uma “noção mística”. Quero estar em paz com o não conhecer, tendo a consciência disso, preservando-a, sem criar um conhecimento místico ou imaginário para preencher o lugar. Bem pior do que a ignorância é a informação errada. Seria uma discussão para ter, entre a ignorância e a informação errada. Quem é ignorante, significa que não quis aprender sobre um qualquer tema. Quem é errante, significa que quer aprender sobre um qualquer tema. Se nesta vida, para sempre iremos aprender, só quem não erra é que não pode aprender. A ignorância não vem necessariamente de não querer aprender. Em muita coisa que ignoramos nem sequer fomos confrontados com essa possibilidade, simplesmente desconhecemos em absoluto a sua existência. Noutros casos sim, optamos por não saber mais, o que é perfeitamente justificável, face ao tempo finito que dispomos de vida e também, à nossa reduzida capacidade de armazenamento de informação. Aquele que quis aprender sobre algo e fez um esforço válido nesse sentido, pode mesmo assim permanecer ignorante sobre a totalidade da matéria, ou até mesmo errar sobre aquilo que sabe, mas isso é bem diferente de não ter preocupação nenhuma. Não fazer esforço para adquirir conhecimento certo e simplesmente inventar noções místicas sobre o tema. Não discordando, tenho uma opinião diferente quanto à especulação da probabilidade, face ao desconhecimento e ao inexplicável. É que, todo o ser que procurou compreendeer, especulou sobre a probabilidade, sendo que uma maioria terá lido sobre o conteúdo que queria conhecer, os que acabaram por ensinar, aprenderam via essa especulação que inventa probabilidades, como apontadores de verdades. O misticismo não é mais do que essa sensação de estranheza, aquando confrontados com o desconhecido, sendo que a mística é uma disciplina humana, isto é, do foro da sensibilidade humana. Foi assim que a ciência andou durante séculos. Como poderia um cientísta acreditar que a dor expressa pelo cão que está a ser violatado, é uma resposta mecânica e como tal, o animal não sente nem tem emoções? O Big Bang também poderá ser misticismo e especulação, de quem é capaz de imaginar e a partir daí, criar. Novas teorias, verdadeiras ou falsas pouco interessa para esta resposta, mas interessa sim, sublinhar a capacidade de criar a partir do que já conhecia. E por isso, sendo que a teoria do Big Bang é especulatória, ela faz parte da mística, isto é, de uma tentativa de explicar algo que continua a não ter explicação e por isso, entre “deus criou” ou “um atmo explodiu”, ambas as afirmações são verdadeiras e falsas ao mesmo tempo. O que seria da filosofia sem essa tentantiva racional de encontrar uma explicação do abstrato e da realidade? Dai que todas as teorias filosóficas, poderão ser somente especulações, sendo que são apontadores, perspectivas. Por isso, entre a visão puramente racional, que se desliga do ser que sente e que tem capacidade de imaginar e como tal, criar, gosto da perspectiva criativa, que atribuí simbologia e significado ao que já existe como evento, para explicar o que nessa perspectiva criativa, é possível compreender. [Só tentou criar uma explicação criativa, sendo que a puramente racional, também o é, mas a linguagem é mais abstracta do que objectiva. Curiosamente] Uma crença em algo sobrenatural ou misterioso, só porque sim, é diferente da formulação de hipóteses e das posteriores tentativas, feitas para procurar verificar a sua possível validação como a ciência o faz. É claro que a especulação está presente nessa formulação mas são cenários diferentes. O cenário é igual, pois é simplesmente alguém a tentar explicar algo, sendo que a formulação é diferente. Portanto, o que muda é simplesmente a forma de explicar, sendo que nesse aspecto, continuo a gostar das duas formulas. Não é relativo a algo “sobrenatural”, mas natural, que por desconhecimento o torna místerioso. As galáxias e os buracos negros, nada têm de “sobrenatural”, sendo que os efeitos dos seus eventos, cria aos atentos, sensações corporais que traduzem o tal lado “místico”. Pessoalmente relaciono o “místico” ao lado puramente sensorial, isto é, animal, que é também o que somos. Naturalmente que não nego o lado “racional”, sendo esse lado pouco animal. É o que tentamos ser, mas nem sempre somos capazes de ser. Os objectos cãem porque: “Assim quer o Grande Espírito” O potencial desta teoria ser verdadeira é simplísta, mas a formula que a explica é objectiva. mongodb: ≡ M MongoDB / Field Manual 00 / 17 Home Field manual · Rev. 2026.10 · Single-node deployment MongoDB, from zero to hero A gated, command-line-first technical manual for installing, hardening, backing up and operating MongoDB on one dedicated Linux machine. Most MongoDB outages are not caused by MongoDB. They are caused by a database reachable from the internet with no authentication, a backup that was never restored, an unbounded array, or an index that nobody measured. This manual walks you through every one of those failure modes in the order you would actually meet them — and refuses to unlock the next level until you can prove you understood the last one. Target version MongoDB 8.0 LTS (9.0 notes inline) Platform Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04 x86_64 or arm64 Levels 17 + capstone 60 questions Interface Shell, mongosh & config files External assets None. One file. No CDN, no fonts. § Front matter 6 min How this manual works This is a linear document on purpose. MongoDB is unusually easy to start and unusually easy to misconfigure; the dangerous settings only make sense after you understand the safe ones. So the manual is split into seventeen levels across five tiers, and each level ends with a gate : three questions you must answer correctly to unlock the next level. TIER I Foundations → 00 model TIER II Build → 01 machine → 02 install → 03 config → 04 shell TIER III Use → 05 CRUD → 06 schema → 07 indexes → 08 aggregation TIER IV Harden → 09 replica set → 10 auth → 11 TLS → 12 backups → 13 ops TIER V Reference → 14 drivers → 15 commands → 16 GUI ★ Capstone → 12 questions across everything ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Each arrow is a gate. A gate is not a formality: it is the point. The rules Work in order. Gates unlock sequentially. If you already know a level, the quiz takes ninety seconds. Run the commands. Every command block is real, copyable, and was written against MongoDB 8.0 on Ubuntu. Read the output blocks too — that is where the diagnosis lives. Read the red boxes. Each level contains at least one Bad decision callout. Those are the expensive lessons, explained rather than just prohibited. Progress is local. Your cleared levels are kept in localStorage under this browser profile. Clear it, lose it. Nothing is sent anywhere. No external assets. This entire manual — layout, styles, quizzes, syntax highlighting — is one index.html with zero network requests after load. ◆ Conventions used below Commands prefixed with $ run as your normal user; # means root or sudo . Output is shown in grey after the command. Placeholders look like <THIS> . Values you must not commit are written as REPLACE_ME . The mongosh prompt is shortened to rs0 [primary] app> so you always know which database and role you are in. ⚠ What this manual is not This is a single-machine deployment: one mongod , one host, no sharding, no second data-bearing member. That is a legitimate architecture for internal tools, CI, edge deployments and small production workloads — but it is a single point of failure, and no amount of configuration changes that. Where redundancy would normally be the answer, this manual says so explicitly instead of pretending a single node is highly available. You will, however, still run a single-node replica set , because that is what unlocks transactions, retryable writes and oplog-based backups. Prerequisites You need Minimum Comfortable Why OS Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Official .deb repositories and systemd units. RHEL/Debian notes are in Level 2. CPU 2 vCPU 4+ vCPU WiredTiger compression and index builds are CPU-bound. RAM 2 GB 8–16 GB WiredTiger cache defaults to 50% of (RAM − 1 GB). Disk 20 GB SSD XFS on dedicated SSD/NVMe Never use network storage for the journal; never fill the disk. Access sudo SSH key + non-root admin You will run mongod as a dedicated unprivileged user. Network Outbound HTTPS Private interface only To fetch packages. Inbound 27017 stays closed to the internet. Table 0.1 — Baseline for the machine you are about to build. Numbers are for a small production database, not a laptop demo. If you are missing a machine, any Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 VM works — a local hypervisor, a cloud instance, or a spare box. Everything from Level 1 onward assumes you can ssh into it and that it is dedicated : MongoDB gets the machine, and the application that uses it lives somewhere else. ✓ How to read a gate Answer all three questions, press Validate , and you get per-question explanations whether you pass or fail. You need all three correct to unlock the next level. Wrong answers are marked, explanations open, and you can retry immediately. Guessing your way through is possible; it is also the fastest way to arrive at Level 12 without knowing what a mongodump --oplog actually protects you from. 00 Tier I · Foundations 14 min The document model, without the marketing Before you install anything, you need a correct mental model of what MongoDB stores. Almost every bad MongoDB schema is a relational schema wearing a JSON costume. MongoDB is a document database. The unit of storage is a BSON document — a binary encoding of an ordered set of field/value pairs that looks like JSON but carries more types. Documents live in collections ; collections live in a database ; a running server process is mongod . There are no tables, no rows, no foreign keys, and no schema enforced by default. instance (mongod) └── database "shop" namespace prefix; auth boundary ├── collection "orders" no fixed schema, per-collection indexes │ ├── document { _id, customer, lines[], total, status } │ ├── document { _id, customer, lines[], total, status } │ └── document { _id, customer, lines[], total, status, refund? } └── collection "customers" └── document { _id, email, addresses[] } A real order document, exactly as you would insert it in Level 5: javascript mongosh · shop.orders copy { _id: ObjectId("66f1c0a2b7d4e91f3c8a1201"), orderNumber: "ORD-2026-000871", customer: { id: ObjectId("66f1b9e0b7d4e91f3c8a1188"), email: "ana.torres@example.com", country: "ES" }, placedAt: ISODate("2026-10-14T09:12:44.318Z"), lines: [ { sku: "KB-88-BRN", name: "Keyboard 88", qty: 1, unitPrice: Decimal128("129.00") }, { sku: "CB-USBC-2M", name: "USB-C cable 2 m", qty: 2, unitPrice: Decimal128("11.50") } ], total: Decimal128("152.00"), currency: "EUR", status: "paid", tags: ["priority", "gift-wrap"], payment: { method: "card", last4: "4242", capturedAt: ISODate("2026-10-14T09:12:51.002Z") } } Everything the application needs to render an order page is in one read. That is the entire point of the model: locality. You are optimising for "fetch the thing I display" instead of "store each fact exactly once". BSON is not JSON BSON adds types JSON lacks, and those types matter operationally. Store money as Decimal128 or integer cents, never as a float; store time as a real date, never as a string. A field's type is part of your schema even when MongoDB does not enforce one. BSON type mongosh constructor Use it for Do not use it for ObjectId ObjectId() Default _id ; 12 bytes, roughly time-ordered Anything you need to guess; it is not a secret String "text" Names, enums, SKUs, ISO country codes Dates, numbers you will sort or sum Int32 / Int64 NumberInt(5) , Long("5") Counters, milliseconds, integer cents Money with fractions; timestamps as magic numbers Double 1.5 (default) Measurements, scores, geo coordinates Currency, invoice totals Decimal128 Decimal128("129.00") Money, tax, anything audited to the cent High-volume arithmetic where speed dominates Date ISODate() , new Date() All timestamps. Always UTC on the server. Local wall-clock times without an offset Timestamp Timestamp() Internal oplog ordering Application event times Array [1, 2, 3] Bounded lists: order lines, tags, addresses Unbounded growth (see Level 6) Object { ... } Embedded sub-documents, value objects Deep arbitrary nesting beyond ~100 levels BinData BinData(0, "…") Small blobs, hashes, encrypted payloads Files over 16 MB (use GridFS or object storage) Null / missing null Explicit "no value" Confusing the two: queries treat them differently Table 0.2 — The BSON types you will actually touch. db.orders.insertOne({x: 1.0}) and {x: 1} can both be stored as double; be explicit when the type is load-bearing. The hard limits worth memorising 16 MB maximum BSON document size. This is the constraint that kills unbounded arrays. 100 levels of nesting. You will never hit it intentionally; a recursive import might. 100 MB of memory per blocking aggregation stage, after which it spills to disk (or fails, on versions where allowDiskUse is not the default). 255 bytes practical namespace budget: database.collection plus index names. One _id per document , immutable, unique per collection, indexed automatically. When MongoDB is the wrong tool A manual that only sells you the product is useless. Be honest about the boundary: Workload MongoDB fit Better default Product catalogue, user profiles, CMS, event logs, IoT readings, session stores strong — Financial ledger with many mutually dependent tables and heavy ad-hoc joins awkward PostgreSQL Full-text search over millions of documents with relevance tuning limited Atlas Search, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Petabyte analytics with columnar scans wrong ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake Strict multi-row invariants enforced by the database itself possible RDBMS with constraints; MongoDB has schema validation but no foreign keys Single-node hobby app with one writer fine — (but still read Level 12) ✕ Bad decision · "MongoDB is MySQL with JSON columns" The most expensive mistake in this entire manual, because it is made on day one and discovered on year two. Teams port a normalised schema directly: a users collection, an orders collection, an order_items collection, a products collection. Then every page load fires four queries and joins them in application code, because MongoDB has no JOIN in the CRUD layer. Why it hurts: you pay network round-trips for data that was always displayed together; you lose atomicity across those writes unless you wrap everything in a transaction (which costs more than the relational database you were avoiding); and $lookup at read time cannot use an index on the foreign collection's join key the way a relational planner can. You end up with the drawbacks of both models. What to do instead: decide the access pattern first . If 95% of reads need the order plus its lines, embed the lines. Keep a reference only for data that is large, shared, or updated independently — the product catalogue, not the line item. Level 6 gives you the decision procedure and the five patterns that cover most cases. ✕ Bad decision · "Schemaless means I do not need to design" MongoDB does not enforce a schema by default, so a collection will happily accept {price: "12.00"} in one document and {price: 12} in the next. Every query that compares or sorts on price then behaves inconsistently, and every aggregation that sums it silently skips the string. Why it hurts: the failure is data-dependent, so it appears in production months later, in one shard of your data, and it is not reproducible locally. Type drift is the single most common "MongoDB bug" that is actually a modelling bug. What to do instead: treat the document shape as a contract and enforce it with $jsonSchema validation (Level 6), plus a schema-version field for migrations. "Flexible" should describe your ability to evolve the schema, not the absence of one. Why is customer partly embedded and partly a reference? What happens at 50,000 order lines in one document? 1. Binary floating point cannot represent 0.10 exactly; summing thousands of doubles produces cent-level drift that fails reconciliation. 2. The email and country are denormalised snapshots needed to render the order without a second query; the id is the durable link. Snapshots are correct here because an order must show the address it was shipped to, not the customer's address today. 3. Clock skew breaks TLS validation, replica-set elections and log correlation. 1.2 Patch, then pin bash root copy sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get -y upgrade sudo apt-get -y install chrony ca-certificates curl gnupg jq sudo systemctl enable --now chrony chronyc tracking | head -3 Reference ID : A9FEA9FE (time.cloudflare.com) Stratum : 3 System time : 0.000031 seconds fast of NTP time ⚠ Pin the database, patch the OS Automatic unattended upgrades are good for OpenSSL and the kernel, and bad for your database engine. A silent major-version jump of mongodb-org at 03:00 is an outage with a confusing cause. If they share a volume with the OS and the OS fills up, mongod stops accepting writes — and a full disk is the most common self-inflicted MongoDB outage after an open port. Path Contents Growth Recommended /var/lib/mongodb Data files ( .wt ), WiredTiger , diagnostic.data Steady, proportional to data + indexes Dedicated XFS volume, noatime /var/log/mongodb mongod.log Slow, but unbounded without rotation Same disk is fine — with rotation /var/backups/mongodb Temporary dumps Spiky, can double your footprint Only as staging; copy off-host /etc/mongod.conf Configuration Bytes Version-controlled (no secrets in it) Table 1.1 — The only four paths that matter. On a cloud VM, attach a separate volume for /var/lib/mongodb so you can grow or re-attach it without rebuilding the host. If you do have a second volume, format it as XFS and mount it. Skip this if /var/lib/mongodb is already on a suitably sized XFS root ; do not invent a volume just to follow along. bash example: /dev/nvme1n1 as the data volume copy # 1. Confirm the device is empty and not mounted. This destroys data. lsblk -f /dev/nvme1n1 # 2. XFS, labelled, mounted with noatime sudo mkfs.xfs -L mongodb-data /dev/nvme1n1 sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/mongodb # 3. Persist the mount (adjust to your device's UUID or path) echo 'LABEL=mongodb-data /var/lib/mongodb xfs defaults,noatime 0 2' | \ sudo tee -a /etc/fstab sudo mount -a findmnt /var/lib/mongodb TARGET SOURCE FSTYPE OPTIONS /var/lib/mongodb /dev/nvme1n1 xfs rw,noatime,attr2,inode64,logbufs=8 1.4 Tune the kernel for a database, not a desktop bash root copy # Keep the database resident; only swap under real pressure echo 'vm.swappiness = 1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-mongodb.conf echo 'vm.max_map_count = 262144' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-mongodb.conf sudo sysctl --system # NUMA: MongoDB recommends running with interleaved memory on multi-socket hosts numactl --hardware | head -3 available: 2 nodes (0-1) node 0 cpus: 0 1 2 3 ... The internet will not. Set the default policy first and open only SSH and — later, restricted — MongoDB. bash ufw copy sudo apt-get -y install ufw sudo ufw default deny incoming sudo ufw default allow outgoing sudo ufw allow 22/tcp comment 'ssh' # Allow MongoDB only from the application subnet. Your admin login owns the host; the mongodb OS user (created by the package) owns the data directory and runs mongod . Never run the database as root . Time and logs. UTC everywhere. moreMusicTheory: ◖)) Sound & the Brain A psychology field guide · sound, memory & choice A sound passes. Its meaning can stay. A voice, a song, a warning chime: sound is vibration reaching the ear, but what it means is shaped by a living brain—by attention, learning, memory, emotion, body, culture, and context. 01 From air movement to experience Sound is physical. Hearing is biological. Meaning is interpreted. In air, a sound wave is a traveling pattern of compressions and rarefactions. The air itself does not fly from the source to your ear; local particles oscillate as the pressure disturbance passes. The eardrum and middle-ear bones transmit movement to the fluid-filled cochlea. Hair cells convert that mechanical movement into neural signals, which travel through auditory pathways to the brain. Sound source vibrates → Air pressure wave travels → Ear & cochlea motion becomes neural activity Brain networks analyze patterns ← Context & memory shape interpretation ← Attention selects what matters There is no single “sound meaning” switch. The simplified diagram is a teaching map: auditory processing happens at multiple levels and interacts with attention, expectation, memory, and other brain systems. The physics boundary “Everything vibrates” needs precision Earth is made of matter, and matter can move or oscillate at many scales. The planet can ring in seismic modes after very large earthquakes; molecules in matter also have motion. But that does not mean every object is continuously making audible sound, sharing one special frequency, or responding to sound in the same way. Audible sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium. Earth’s atmosphere carries sound; outer space is mostly vacuum, so ordinary sound does not travel through it as it does through air. Seismic waves in the solid Earth are vibrations too, but they are not the same thing as audible air pressure waves. The psychology boundary A cue can influence—not dictate Brains detect patterns and use learned expectations. A sound may draw attention, signal a likely event, evoke a feeling, or prompt an action. Those are probabilities shaped by situation and learning, not proof that one frequency programs a fixed behavior. People differ. A siren might mean danger to one person, a job to another, and a film scene to someone else. Even for one person, the response may change with safety, context, fatigue, and time. 02 Words have a melody; music has a story How we say something can add information beyond the words themselves. Speech · prosody Voice is more than vocabulary Pitch movement, timing, rhythm, emphasis, loudness, and pauses—together called prosody —help listeners infer emphasis, phrase boundaries, questions, and a speaker’s possible affect. We interpret those cues alongside the actual words and the situation. pitch contour stress timing pauses Music · expectation The brain listens ahead As music unfolds, listeners learn style-specific patterns and form expectations. A continuation, a rhythmic change, or a return may feel rewarding or moving in part because of how it plays with prediction and attention. This is one account of musical pleasure, not a complete explanation for every listener. Familiarity, culture, bodily response, memory, and the moment all contribute too. Emotion · not a decoder ring Recognizing ≠ feeling You can recognize that music sounds sad without feeling sad yourself. A bright voice does not prove happiness; a loud voice does not prove anger. Acoustic cues can inform interpretation, but they are not infallible labels for someone's inner state. Words, context, speaker, listener, and culture change what cues mean. Why a sound can make us laugh—or cry A song linked to a person, place, or past event can act as a retrieval cue. It may bring back a scene, a bodily feeling, or the sense of a particular time in life. A familiar melody can also create emotion through expectation and the way musical events unfold—even without a specific autobiographical memory. These routes may overlap, but no song is guaranteed to evoke the same response in everyone. A vivid memory feels powerful; vividness alone does not certify every detail. Remembering is reconstructive, not a perfect audio-video replay. Emotion can make some aspects memorable while leaving other details uncertain. Treat this as a reason for care—not as a reason to dismiss someone's memory. 03 Memory is a network, not a sound file A cue can reopen a path to associations, but it does not replay the past exactly. A cue can connect several things A familiar sound may become associated with people, places, routines, expectations, and emotions. Hearing it later may retrieve part of that network. What comes to mind depends on the person's history and the present context. A ringtone that repeatedly comes before an important call may grab attention; a song heard during a joyful gathering may become a warm reminder. A cue paired with a distressing event may instead bring unease. These examples describe possible learned links, not a diagnosis. Cues do not affect all people alike, and a learned response can vary or change with later experience. A person's “first choice” is not necessarily a fixed, natural default written by one sound-memory. A sound-triggered reaction can be real without being inevitable, permanent, or fully explained by the sound alone. 04 From sound to behavior: the learning loop A useful chain to notice—not a claim that stimulus automatically causes action. sound / cue → attention & meaning → feeling / body state → possible response → what happens next Learning can connect a cue with what tends to follow. A chime may remind someone to check a message; a beat may invite movement; an alarm may prompt action. Repeated consequences can make a response more likely in a particular context. But a person can notice the cue, interpret it differently, pause, or choose another response. Possible supports Music can help some people feel energized, connected, comforted, or focused in some circumstances. A familiar song may cue autobiographical memories. Rhythm can make movement feel easier or more engaging for some tasks. Possible costs Unwanted or loud noise can interrupt communication, rest, and concentration. Lyrics may compete with reading or verbal memory. A sound associated with threat or loss may be uncomfortable. Effects depend on dose, timing, task, and the person. “Music boosts memory” is too broad. In one study of college students, lyrics impaired tested verbal memory, visual memory, and reading comprehension compared with silence; tested instrumental lo-fi music did not reliably help or harm those tasks.
